title: Contemporary screen time usage among children 9-10-years-old is associated with higher body mass index percentile at 1-year follow-up: A prospective cohort study
authors: Nagata JM, Iyer P, Chu J, Baker FC, Pettee Gabriel K, Garber AK, Murray SB, Bibbins-Domingo K, Ganson KT

primary_models.name: Weighted multiple linear regression of 1-year follow-up BMI percentile on baseline phone/SM hours per day (texting, video chat, social networking), fully adjusted including baseline BMI percentile
primary_models.location_in_paper: Table 2, right-hand columns 'BMI percentile at follow-up, fully adjusted' (Model 2) (p. 4); reported in Results p. 3 and Abstract; interpreted in Discussion pp. 3-4.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort with two waves. Screen time exposures measured at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10); the outcome, BMI percentile, measured once at the 1-year follow-up (2017-2019, ages 10-11). Baseline BMI percentile is entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline BMI percentile. Single follow-up outcome, not repeated measures; no time interaction. Each screen modality was examined in a separate regression model (Table 2 note: 14 regression models in total across the 7 exposures x 2 adjustment levels).
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 3.0, baseline and 1-year follow-up. Of 11,875 children recruited at 21 U.S. sites, participants missing baseline screen time (N = 63) or 1-year follow-up BMI (N = 752) were excluded, leaving N = 11,066. Missing covariate data (N = 1016) were singly imputed by Gaussian normal regression. Baseline age mean 9.9 (SD 0.6); 48.8% female, 51.2% male; 52.2% White, 20.0% Latino/Hispanic, 17.3% Black, 5.5% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.9% Other. Household income: 18.7% <$25,000; 20.4% $25,000-49,999; 17.5% $50,000-74,999; 13.4% $75,000-99,999; 22.6% $100,000-199,999; 7.4% >=$200,000. 79.7% had a parent with college education or more. Major depressive disorder 0.2%; binge-eating disorder 0.7%. Baseline BMI category: 3.9% underweight, 62.5% normal, 15.9% overweight, 17.8% obese (Table 1, propensity-weighted).
primary_models.iv: Baseline hours per day on each phone/SM modality, each entered in a separate model: texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, Facetime), and social networking (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Instrument: ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey, child self-report of typical hours per day, asked separately for weekdays and weekend days; a weighted average of weekday and weekend use gives a typical-day value, analyzed as continuous hours per day. Baseline means (SD), Table 1: texting 0.24 (0.56); video chat 0.21 (0.52); social networking 0.13 (0.45) h/day.
primary_models.dv: BMI percentile at 1-year follow-up. BMI computed from the average of two to three research-staff measurements of height and weight (kg/m^2) and converted to sex- and age-specific percentiles using CDC growth curves. Table 1: follow-up BMI percentile mean 63.5 (SD 30.5); baseline BMI percentile mean 62.1 (SD 30.7).

primary_models.equation: BMIpct_Y1[i] = b0 + b1*phoneSM_IV_baseline[i] + b2*BMIpct_baseline[i] + b3..*race_ethnicity + b*sex + b*household_income + b*parent_education + b*depression + b*binge_eating_disorder + b*site + e[i], where phoneSM_IV is one of texting, video chat, or social networking hours/day (one model per IV).
primary_models.estimation: Multiple linear regression in Stata 15.1 (analysis performed in 2020). ABCD pre-constructed propensity weights based on the American Community Survey were applied. Single imputation by Gaussian normal regression for missing covariates. Site entered as a covariate; no family clustering, but a sensitivity analysis including only one sibling per family gave similar findings (numbers not printed). Significance at p < 0.05 (bold in Table 2); no multiple-comparison correction reported. Effect modification of screen time by sex was tested and was not present (p for interaction > 0.05); no stratified estimates reported. Appendices A and B (online supporting information, not in this PDF) repeat the analyses with BMI and BMI z-score as outcomes.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1)
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 hour/day of the phone/SM modality, rescaled to per 1 SD of the IV
d_transformation.notes: SD_IV from Table 1 (p. 3), baseline screen time hours per day for the analytic N = 11,066: texting 0.56, video chat 0.52, social networking 0.45. SD_DV = 30.5, the SD of BMI percentile at 1-year follow-up in Table 1 (p. 3). Table 1 values are propensity-weighted. Because baseline BMI percentile is a covariate, B reflects association with follow-up BMI percentile net of baseline; standardizing by the raw follow-up SD (not a residual/change SD) yields a very small d and is not directly comparable to cross-sectional estimates. IVs are heavily floor-skewed (means under 15 min/day). [complete stage] Re-verified all inputs against Table 1/Table 2; no supplement file in docs/pdfs (Appendices A-B are online Supporting Information only).

extraction_flags: The PDF is the 5-page short communication only. Appendices A and B are online supporting information that was not available, so the per-modality sensitivity estimates for BMI and BMI z-score were not extracted. Site is listed as a covariate, but the paper does not say whether it is a fixed effect or a random effect. Age is not among the covariates; this is presumably because BMI percentile is already age- and sex-specific. SD_DV is the raw SD of follow-up BMI percentile (30.5), but the model adjusts for baseline BMI percentile, so the derived d values will be very small and are not comparable to cross-sectional d values. The SDs in Table 1 are propensity-weighted. The social networking estimate was not significant (p=0.075). Texting and video chat were significant.
